top.title: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain
top.summary: A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A may help the brain get more oxygen and nutrients when it needs them most. In a randomized clinical trial involving 50 middle-aged adults with obesity, researchers found that taking the supplement daily for four weeks increased blood flow to the brain during a challenging memory task, particularly in a region involved in working memory.
top.text: A dietary supplement known as urolithin A may help the brain meet its increased demand for oxygen and nutrients during mentally challenging activities. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Oklahoma, middle-aged adults with obesity who took the supplement experienced increased blood flow to the brain while performing a memory task. The findings, published in JAMA Network Open , could shed new light on how urolithin A influences blood vessel function and brain health. Obesity can affect how blood vessels function, potentially disrupting circulation throughout the body and brain. To investigate whether urolithin A could help counter these effects, the research team recruited 50 adults with obesity between the ages of 40 and 64 for a randomized clinical trial. For four weeks, participants took either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A each day or a placebo. During a demanding memory exercise, participants who received urolithin A showed a greater increase in brain blood flow than those in the placebo group. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area that plays an important role in working memory, the ability to temporarily hold and process information. However, the researchers observed no significant improvement in blood vessel function in the arm or in participants' performance on memory tests. According to the research team, this is the first study in humans to document an effect of urolithin A on the function of blood vessels in the brain. "The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity," said the study's first author, Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. "We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health." The human body can produce urolithin A with the help of certain gut bacteria. These microorganisms generate the substance by breaking down naturally occurring compounds in foods such as pomegranates, strawberries, and walnuts. Not everyone produces the same amount of urolithin A. Previous research suggests that the ability to generate the compound naturally tends to diminish as people grow older and their body mass index increases, Langley explained. Urolithin A can also be obtained directly through dietary supplements. Participants tolerated the supplement well throughout the trial. However, the researchers cautioned that the study involved a relatively small number of people at a single research site. Larger, longer clinical trials will be necessary to better understand the supplement's effects. Although the increase in brain blood flow is encouraging, it remains unclear whether this change could translate into lasting improvements in cognitive health. "These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain," said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. "Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits." For Langley, the broader aim is to extend healthspan, the portion of a person's life spent in good health. "The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline," she said. "We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives." Materials provided by University of Oklahoma . Note: Content may be edited for style and length. top.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
top.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.
top.text: Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them. The gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play important roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the new findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years. To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them. The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome. These medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions. "Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as important as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author. This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an important part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another. One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety. Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system. The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria. This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication. Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants. By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients. Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections. Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought The findings point to an important consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier. If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed. The results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems. "This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data." Materials provided by Estonian Research Council . top.title: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 25 years as vaccine myths persist
top.summary: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, and a new survey reveals widespread misconceptions about the deadly disease and its vaccine. With measles cases surging, more than one-third of Americans still believe or are uncertain about the debunked vaccine-autism link, while most don't know the disease's risks or how many vaccine doses children need.
top.text: The United States has lost its measles elimination status after more than 25 years, marking a major setback in the fight against a highly contagious disease. At the same time, a new nationwide survey from the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) reveals that many Americans remain confused about the dangers of measles and the vaccines that protect against it. The United States first achieved measles elimination status in 2000. This designation meant that no strain of the virus had spread continuously within the country for 12 months or longer. However, on Nov. 17, 2026, the Pan American Health Organization confirmed that the United States no longer qualified for that status. The announcement comes during the country's worst measles resurgence in decades. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United States had recorded 5,412 confirmed cases in 2026 as of Nov. 12. That is more than twice the 2,290 cases reported throughout all of 2025. A November 2026 Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) survey, conducted using adults from the SSRS Omnibus survey, highlights widespread misunderstandings about childhood vaccination. Nearly two-thirds of Americans (64%) correctly rejected the claim that "vaccines given to children for diseases like measles, mumps, and rubella cause autism." However, 17% believed the claim was true, while another 19% said they did not know whether it was true or false. The results closely resemble findings from earlier APPC research. Across four surveys involving a separate sample of U.S. adults (September 2024 to August 2026), the ongoing ASAPH national probability survey found that 65% to 68% correctly rejected a connection between childhood vaccines and autism (65%-68%). Another 12% to 14% incorrectly believed there was a connection (12%-14%), while 19% to 22% remained uncertain. The latest survey also asked respondents to compare autism rates among fully vaccinated and unvaccinated children. Nearly half (49%) believed both groups were "about as likely" to show signs of autism. Another 11% thought fully vaccinated children were "more likely" to show signs, 14% believed they were "less likely," and 26% could not say. Extensive scientific research has found no evidence that vaccines cause autism. In 2004, the National Academy of Medicine (then named the Institute of Medicine) concluded that "the body of epidemiological evidence favors rejection of a causal relationship between the MMR vaccine and autism evidence." The World Health Organization's Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety reached the same conclusion in 2025, reaffirming that high-quality scientific evidence does not establish a causal relationship between vaccination and autism. FactCheck.org, which is operated by the Annenberg Public Policy Center, has also challenged claims linking vaccines to autism, explaining that the evidence does not support them. These misconceptions may have consequences for vaccination decisions. Previous Annenberg research found that people who accept false vaccine claims, including the belief that the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine causes autism, are less likely to recommend MMR vaccination to people who are eligible to receive it. The survey uncovered another striking knowledge gap. Most Americans appear uncertain about the risk of death associated with measles in children. When asked how many children infected with measles are likely to die from the disease, 59% of respondents said they did not know. Just 9% selected the correct response, "about 1 in 1,000," which most closely matches the CDC’s estimate that 1 to 3 of every 1,000 infected children die from respiratory or neurological complications. Nearly one-quarter of respondents (23%) underestimated the death rate, while another 9% selected a higher rate. Knowledge about measles vaccination was also limited. Almost half of Americans (49%) said they were unsure how many doses children need for full protection. Only about one-third (34%) correctly identified the recommended two-dose schedule. The CDC advises giving children their first MMR vaccine dose between 12 and 15 months of age, followed by a second dose between ages 4 and 6. According to CDC data , a single dose provides 93% protection against measles, while receiving both doses increases effectiveness to 97%. The survey also examined Americans' trust in U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The findings indicate that public confidence in his health-related communications has changed little since earlier surveys conducted in 2025 and 2026. In November 2026, about six in 10 respondents (61%) said they were not confident that Kennedy was providing trustworthy information about public health. The remaining four in 10 (39%) expressed confidence in the information he provides. These results are consistent with seven earlier national probability surveys conducted over two years (February 2025 to August 2026). During that period, 60% to 63% of respondents reported lacking confidence in Kennedy, while 37% to 39% expressed confidence. Kathleen Hall Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Public Policy Center's Science of Science Communication Institute and its ASAPH and ASK surveys, said the loss of measles elimination status demonstrates the consequences of declining vaccination coverage. "The announcement that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status confirms what we already knew," said Kathleen Hall Jamieson. "Those who refused the MMR vaccine for themselves or their children and those who misled them into doing so have produced the tragic effects that science predicted would occur when community immunity dropped below the threshold needed to protect those who are not able to be vaccinated or refused to be." The findings draw on two types of Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) surveys. The November 2026 results come from a nationally representative survey of 1,028 U.S. adults conducted for APPC by SSRS, an independent market research organization. Participants were selected from the company's probability-based online opinion panel, and responses were collected Nov. 6-8, 2026. The survey has a margin of sampling error (MOE) of ± 3.5 percentage points at the 95% confidence level. The other findings come from APPC's ongoing ASAPH panel surveys, which are also administered by SSRS. Participants were originally recruited through probability sampling from the SSRS Opinion Panel, and their responses are weighted to reflect the U.S. adult population. This research panel operates separately from the SSRS Omnibus survey and has completed more than 30 survey waves since April 2021. Percentages are rounded to the nearest whole number, so totals may not always equal 100%. Additional results are available in the survey topline , which includes data from both the November 2026 omnibus survey and the ongoing ASAPH panel surveys. A separate methodology statement provides further details about the latest survey. Since April 2021, the Annenberg Public Policy Center has used its Annenberg Science and Public Health (ASAPH) research program and separate national samples to monitor Americans' knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to vaccines, Covid-19, influenza, RSV, and other important health issues. The APPC health survey team includes Ken Winneg, managing director of survey research; Laura A. Gibson, research analyst; and Patrick E. Jamieson, director of the Annenberg Health and Risk Communication Institute. Materials provided by Annenberg Public Policy Center of the University of Pennsylvania . top.title: A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way
top.summary: A surprising discovery suggests the Milky Way may be making stars in places where most galaxies cannot. Scientists found evidence that a massive rotating structure near the galactic center is creating powerful shock waves that trigger star formation rather than suppress it. Even more unexpectedly, part of the Norma spiral arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a vast region where new stars are being born.
top.text: New research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else. The discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow new stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth. Published in Nature Astronomy , the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth. Lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, said the research provides new insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them. "At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis said. "In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed." The Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar. As the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air. Studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center. "The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis said. "As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated." Observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of new stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars. However, the new findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar. "We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis said. To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming. A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths. By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations. "We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar. "This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she said. The possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way. Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself. Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging. "Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis said. The team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly. The results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way. "By comparing a new generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis said. top.title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
top.summary: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.
top.text: A familiar dietary supplement combined with low-dose aspirin may offer an unexpected alternative to antibiotics for people with severe gum disease. In a year-long clinical trial, patients who received omega-3 and aspirin alongside conventional periodontal treatment experienced nearly identical clinical benefits to those who received antibiotics. Perhaps even more surprisingly, the improvements were still evident six months after supplementation ended. The findings, published in the Journal of Periodontology , come from researchers affiliated with Albert Einstein Israelite Hospital, Guarulhos University (UNG), the University of Taubaté (UNITAU), and the Ribeirão Preto School of Dentistry at USP (FORP-USP) in Brazil, as well as Harvard University in the United States. The study suggests that combining omega-3 with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), better known as aspirin, could reduce the need for antibiotics in certain patients. The discovery is particularly timely given growing worldwide concerns about antibiotic resistance, which occurs when bacteria develop the ability to survive exposure to drugs designed to kill them. Researchers monitored 109 patients with advanced periodontitis over 12 months. Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease that develops when bacteria accumulate below the gumline, triggering an immune response that can gradually damage the tissues and bone that hold teeth in place. Without proper treatment, the disease can cause teeth to loosen and eventually fall out. As periodontitis progresses, spaces known as periodontal pockets form between the teeth and gums. These pockets can become increasingly deep, making it difficult to remove harmful bacteria through ordinary brushing and flossing. "Patients with severe disease have very deep pockets, which act as reservoirs for bacteria associated with the disease. It's a very challenging condition to treat," says dental surgeon Nídia Cristina Castro dos Santos, the first author of the study and a professor and researcher at Einstein. The researchers randomly divided the participants into four treatment groups. Every patient received subgingival instrumentation, commonly referred to as scaling. This standard periodontal treatment involves removing bacterial deposits and hardened plaque from tooth surfaces beneath the gums. Each group also received a different complementary treatment. Patients in the control group received inactive substitutes for the antibiotics, omega-3, and aspirin, supplied in capsules that looked identical to those containing the active treatments. A second group received metronidazole and amoxicillin three times daily for 14 days. This combination of antibiotics has some of the strongest scientific evidence supporting its use as an additional treatment for severe periodontitis. Participants in the third group took three grams of omega-3 each day, together with a daily dose of low-dose aspirin, for six months. The fourth group received both interventions, taking antibiotics for two weeks while following the six-month omega-3 and aspirin regimen. The researchers assessed the patients' progress at three, six, and 12 months. At the end of the study, approximately 58% of patients in the antibiotic group had reached the researchers' clinical treatment target, defined as having no more than four remaining deep periodontal pockets. The omega-3 and aspirin group achieved an almost identical success rate of 57.7%. By comparison, only 23.1% of patients who underwent scaling and received placebos reached the same target. Interestingly, administering both antibiotics and the omega-3 and aspirin regimen together did not produce any additional benefits. Although antibiotics can improve treatment outcomes in patients with particularly severe gum disease, they are not routinely necessary for everyone with periodontitis. "The use of antibiotics isn't considered the gold standard of treatment. Although metronidazole and amoxicillin yield good results in the most severe cases, their use should be evaluated on a case-by-case basis due to risks related to bacterial resistance and possible adverse effects," says Castro dos Santos. The findings build on earlier research into the potential role of omega-3 fatty acids in protecting oral health. In a previous investigation, also supported by FAPESP and published in Scientific Reports , scientists found that omega-3 supplementation reduced periodontal inflammation and bone loss in rats. The protective effects were particularly notable when supplementation was combined with physical exercise. Although results from animal studies do not necessarily translate directly to humans, the earlier findings provided clues that omega-3 might help regulate the inflammatory processes that contribute to gum disease. Omega-3 fatty acids are a group of fats found in foods such as oily fish and are widely available as dietary supplements. Beyond their nutritional importance, they serve as building blocks for certain molecules that help regulate inflammation. Castro explains that omega-3 works differently from conventional anti-inflammatory medications. Instead of simply interfering with pathways that promote inflammation, omega-3 helps the body produce molecules involved in bringing inflammation to a natural conclusion and supporting tissue repair. This process, known as the resolution of inflammation, is an active biological mechanism that helps the body return to normal after an immune response. In chronic inflammatory diseases such as periodontitis, inflammation can persist and contribute to ongoing tissue damage. The researchers included low-dose aspirin because it can promote the formation of certain inflammation-resolving molecules. They suspected that combining aspirin with omega-3 could strengthen the body's ability to control the persistent inflammation associated with advanced gum disease. The researchers had originally expected antibiotics and the omega-3 regimen to work best when administered together. Instead, the findings revealed that targeting inflammation could produce clinical improvements comparable to those achieved through antibiotic treatment. "We imagined that the combination of antibiotics and omega-3 would be most effective in controlling periodontitis in these patients. We also believed that the results for the group that used omega-3 with ASA would be slightly lower than those for the antibiotic group. The result was surprising because the two therapies performed very similarly, paving the way for it to become a treatment option for these patients," says Castro. Equally intriguing was how long the improvements lasted. Six months after patients stopped taking omega-3 and aspirin, their clinical outcomes remained similar to those observed when the treatment ended. According to Castro, this persistence raises the possibility that adjusting the body's inflammatory response could have lasting therapeutic effects. However, scientists are still working to understand the biological mechanisms responsible. For dental surgeon Magda Feres, the study's lead author and a full professor at the Harvard School of Dental Medicine and the Graduate Program in Dentistry at UNG, targeting the body's inflammatory response could provide a valuable treatment option for certain patients. "The combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin achieved clinical benefits comparable to those of the metronidazole and amoxicillin protocol, opening up a real alternative for those who can't take antibiotics, especially patients with allergies or intolerance to these medications," she says. The potential to reduce antibiotic use has implications that extend well beyond dentistry. Antibiotic resistance ranks among the greatest threats to global public health, making it increasingly important to identify effective treatment strategies that do not depend on these medications. top.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds
top.summary: Scientists have solved the mystery of strange trenches scattered across Australia’s vast Nullarbor Plain, revealing an extensive hidden world beneath the surface. These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.
top.text: Stretching over 200,000 square kilometers across southern Australia, the vast, flat plains of the Nullarbor mark one of the world’s largest regions of limestone. It formed when an ancient shallow sea retreated some 14 million years ago . Ultimately, this led to the familiar dry landscape of today, which has acted as a significant barrier for plants, animals , and poorly adapted colonial Victorian-era explorers who described it as “ the sort of place one gets into in bad dreams ”. In contrast, the Mirning People of the Nullarbor and Great Australian Bight have lived for tens of thousands of years on this southern margin. They have watched the landscapes change and sea levels fall and rise with the build-up and collapse of the last ice age about 20,000 years ago. To an untrained eye the Nullarbor Plain appears deceptively simple and featureless. However, beneath the immense plain lies a remarkable, largely hidden underground world. Over millions of years, water has eaten away at the limestone and created complex cave networks that can extend for kilometers underground. Sadly, the caves remain poorly understood , partly because they’re only really known and accessible where they breach the surface. Our new study, published in Communications Earth & Environment , reveals a new way to track these cave systems even when they are deeply buried. Our work helps explain the formation of previously mysterious, shallow trench features on the Nullarbor. It also provides a new way to identify hidden caves elsewhere – even beyond our own planet. Scattered across the Nullarbor are tell-tale signs of its vulnerability to being dissolved – small cave openings and shallow depressions. But there are also structures of previously unknown origin and significance: long (up to 20 km), shallow (a few meters) trenches that trend roughly north-south. They’re almost invisible from the ground, but we can clearly see them in modern digital landscape models. These shallow trenches look somewhat like flat-bottomed valleys, but they were not carved by rivers. They begin and end abruptly and are not connected to existing rivers or drainage networks that extend into the upland areas around the Nullarbor. They also lack typical river branching patterns and the sediments within them don’t show any evidence of being deposited from flowing water. To understand how these strange structures formed, we combined several investigative techniques. First, we mapped the trenches using drone and aerial photography, as well as detailed satellite-based digital landscape models. Then the layers of soil and rock were measured in boreholes and caves. Finally, we used specialized geophysical techniques to “see” inside the Earth, somewhat similar to the way an X-ray enables us to see our internal body structures from the outside. The work demonstrated that the shallow surface trenches sit above deep zones of broken rock, and in places line up with known cave systems and sinkholes. This means the trenches are mere muted surface expressions of deeply buried cave systems. These systems are slowly, over millions of years, “collapsing upwards” through the overlying rock layers to reach the surface. The results of this work will change how scientists interpret cave landscapes globally. It shows that to explain the surface structures we see, we must look deeper than we might think. Understanding where voids may exist underground can be important for planning both surface (buildings, roads) and subsurface (tunnels, sewers) engineering works, mitigating geological hazards , and accessing and protecting groundwater resources. Pockmarked karst landscapes (where rocks are dissolved by water, resulting in caves and sinkholes) represent 15% of the ice-free Earth’s surface and supply water to 10–25% of the global population . More fundamentally, caves are important scientific archives . Because caves are sheltered from surface weathering and erosion processes, they can preserve snapshots of ancient environments and ecosystems that would otherwise be lost to time. Furthermore, they may host an array of strange and vulnerable life-forms that have evolved and adapted in isolation . These are some of the least studied organisms on Earth . To learn more, we must first locate the cave structures. And the results of our study could be very important in this regard. The implications of this new work even extend beyond our own planet. Because caves offer a stable environment and shelter from damaging space radiation, they provide promising exploration sites for life on other planets . Mapping of planetary surfaces within our Solar System has identified numerous potential caves, including some thought to be related to karst on Mars . The Nullarbor’s dry, stable surface is an excellent analogue to help locate the subtle surface fingerprints of hidden cave systems on planets that now lack a dynamic water-cycle – such as Mars. Even if the caves are barren of life, they could be attractive bases for future human explorers. How many other apparently simple landscapes around the world or on other planets are concealing large cave systems underneath? We don’t yet know, but the trenches we studied are unlikely to be unique. Similar subtle landforms are likely to have been overlooked elsewhere, too. Sometimes the most remarkable discoveries are waiting in understated but plain view, in landscapes we think we already understand. top.title: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles
top.summary: Researchers have discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage. The molecule, already available as a dietary supplement, could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.
top.text: Researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance. Released during exercise, the molecule could also provide the basis for future treatments to protect against muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity. It helps muscles become stronger, improves their resistance to fatigue, and protects against damage and weakness. The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training. Although the health benefits of exercise are well established, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that allow the body to adapt to physical demands. A research team led by Professor Lee Roberts at the University of Leeds investigated whether these processes could reveal new ways to treat chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes. L-BAIBA has attracted scientific interest for more than a decade. In research published in 2014, Roberts demonstrated that the molecule has beneficial effects on metabolism, helping to enhance the body's ability to burn fat in response to exercise. L-BAIBA is now commercially available as a dietary supplement. The latest findings reveal another important function of the molecule. L-BAIBA acts as a chemical messenger that connects physical activity with beneficial changes in muscle structure and metabolism, helping muscles adapt to the demands placed on them. Lee Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said: "Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance. "This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes." The researchers also discovered that L-BAIBA protects muscles against damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The condition can negatively affect muscle health, leading to a decline in muscle mass and strength, as well as disruptions in the way muscles process and use energy. These complications can significantly reduce a person's quality of life. Because regular physical activity is an important part of managing type 2 diabetes, finding ways to improve muscle function and reduce fatigue could make a substantial difference for people who struggle to exercise. Type 2 diabetes is a serious chronic condition that increases the risk of potentially life-threatening complications, including heart attacks and strokes. Its development is influenced by a complex combination of factors, including age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity. Although type 2 diabetes has traditionally been more common among older adults, diagnoses in people younger than 40 have been rising in recent years. Cases in this younger age group are now increasing more rapidly than among adults over 40. Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: "Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives." Although the discovery opens promising avenues for future treatments, further research is needed to determine whether L-BAIBA supplementation can produce meaningful therapeutic benefits in people with type 2 diabetes. top.title: One type of physical activity is linked to a 20% higher dementia risk
top.summary: A massive study has revealed that exercising for pleasure and performing physical labor at work may have surprisingly different implications for brain health. While recreational exercise was linked to a 24% lower dementia risk, physically demanding work was associated with a 20% higher risk, suggesting that the context of movement matters.
top.text: Regular physical activity has long been recognized as a way to help protect against dementia. However, new research from the University of Southern California (USC) suggests that the circumstances in which people are physically active may be just as important as the amount of activity they get. An analysis involving more than 4.2 million people found that recreational activities such as walking, cycling, running, swimming, and playing sports were associated with a significantly lower risk of dementia. Surprisingly, people who engaged in higher levels of physical activity at work appeared to face an increased risk of developing the condition. Published in The Lancet Public Health , the study is the first systematic investigation into whether a phenomenon known as the "physical activity paradox" also applies to dementia. Already well established in cardiovascular research, this paradox refers to the observation that physical labor does not necessarily offer the same health advantages as recreational exercise and may even be associated with a greater risk of disease. Led by David Raichlen, professor of biological sciences and anthropology at the USC Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences, the research team examined data from 74 cohort and case-control studies. Together, the studies included more than 4.2 million people between the ages of 45 and 93 from 30 countries. Over a median follow-up period of 10 years, researchers monitored diagnoses of all-cause dementia, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia. Participants who engaged in higher levels of recreational physical activity had a 24% lower risk of dementia compared with the least active individuals. Physical activity associated with household chores also appeared to offer benefits, although this finding was supported by only one study. In contrast, higher levels of physical activity at work were linked to a 20% greater risk of dementia. Physically active commuting was also associated with a modest increase in risk, but evidence for this relationship came from just two studies. "The findings challenge the long-held assumption that 'every move counts' for brain health," said Natan Feter, the study's first author, a postdoctoral fellow in Raichlen's Evolutionary Biology of Physical Activity Lab at USC and a researcher in the Graduate Program of Epidemiology at Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (Brazil). Why Exercise and Physical Labor May Affect the Brain Differently Researchers often group recreational exercise, manual labor, household chores, and active commuting together when measuring "Physical activity." However, the authors suggest that the circumstances surrounding these activities vary considerably and could influence their long-term health effects. People who exercise during their free time generally have greater control over the intensity and nature of their activities. Recreational exercise can also provide opportunities to socialize and relieve stress. In comparison, physically demanding occupations may require repeated movements, extended periods of standing, heavy lifting, and insufficient time to recover, along with exposure to potentially harmful workplace conditions. The researchers do not believe that physical movement itself is likely to explain the elevated dementia risk associated with occupational activity. Instead, the relationship may arise from the social and environmental factors commonly associated with manual labor. Physically demanding occupations are more likely to expose workers to psychological and social stress, limited control over their work, unsafe conditions, and higher levels of air and noise pollution. Each of these factors has independently been associated with dementia risk. Workers may also struggle to participate in recreational exercise because of exhaustion, limited free time, or a lack of access to safe spaces for physical activity. The researchers also discovered that the relationship between physical activity and dementia risk was not linear and followed opposite patterns depending on the type of activity. As recreational exercise increased, dementia risk gradually declined until the apparent benefits leveled off. Occupational physical activity showed the reverse pattern, with dementia risk increasing at higher activity levels before eventually reaching a plateau. The authors emphasize that there is still too little research on physical activity related to household chores and commuting to draw definitive conclusions about either. Most of the available evidence also comes from high-income countries, despite projections that low- and middle-income nations will experience the greatest increases in dementia cases in the coming decades. Another limitation is that almost all the studies depended on participants reporting their own physical activity. This approach can introduce errors if people do not accurately remember their activity levels. Nevertheless, Feter said the consistency of the findings across several additional statistical analyses suggests that the observed relationships warrant serious attention. The researchers stress that their findings should not discourage people from pursuing physically active occupations. Since the analysis relied on observational research, it cannot establish that occupational physical activity causes dementia. Instead, the results underscore the importance of examining the conditions under which people are physically active. Recreational exercise continued to be associated with a lower risk of dementia, while occupational activity remained linked to a higher risk even after researchers accounted for differences in age, education, and chronic health conditions. The importance of context may extend beyond physical activity. Separate research by Raichlen, Feter, and their colleagues, published recently in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia , suggests that different types of sedentary behavior may also be associated with differences in brain structure. In that study, mentally stimulating activities performed while sitting, such as working at a desk, were associated with greater volume in certain regions of the cerebral cortex than more passive activities, such as watching television. These differences included brain regions involved in executive function. Together, the findings could have important implications for public health strategies aimed at reducing dementia risk. The authors suggest that encouraging people to "move more" may not be sufficient without also addressing the circumstances in which physical activity takes place. "In other words, when it comes to protecting the brain, the context of physical activity may matter just as much as movement itself," Raichlen said. "Improving access to safe parks, walking trails and recreational facilities, ensuring people have adequate leisure time for exercise, and reducing harmful workplace exposures may ultimately prove as important as promoting physical activity itself." top.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between weak bones and faster brain aging
top.summary: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than scientists previously realized, with new research linking lower spinal bone density to faster cognitive decline and accelerated changes in the brain's white matter. The surprising connection suggests that routine medical scans could help uncover hidden warning signs of brain aging and identify people at increased risk of dementia.
top.text: Weakening bones may reveal more about brain health than previously understood. A new study from Johns Hopkins University found that people with lower bone density in their spine experienced faster cognitive decline and more rapid deterioration of the brain's white matter as they aged. The findings, published in Radiology , a journal of the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA), suggest that bone health and brain aging may be more closely connected than scientists once realized. Bone mineral density reflects how much mineral material, including calcium, is present in a given volume of bone. Lower density makes bones more fragile and increases the likelihood of fractures. Although the effects of bone loss on skeletal health are well established, scientists have conducted relatively little research into how declining bone density might relate to changes in the brain. To explore this connection, a research team led by Sara Momtazmanesh, M.D., a postdoctoral research fellow in the Department of Radiology and Radiological Sciences at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, examined existing data from the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). The analysis included information from participants who had undergone chest CT scans without contrast dye, multiple types of brain MRI examinations, and tests measuring cognitive performance. The researchers applied a deep learning algorithm developed in the laboratory of Shadpour Demehri, M.D., a Johns Hopkins professor of radiology. The AI system analyzed non-contrast chest CT images from 2,086 MESA participants to determine their initial thoracic vertebral volumetric bone mineral density (vBMD), a measurement of bone density in the spine. Of those participants, 715 had the required bone density measurements along with brain MRI results and cognitive testing, making them eligible for the final study group. The researchers examined the MRI scans for two indicators of changes in the brain's white matter. The first was white matter hyperintensities, areas of abnormal tissue that appear unusually bright on certain MRI images. The second was reduced fractional anisotropy, a measurement that can indicate deterioration in the microscopic organization of white matter. Both types of changes have been associated with cognitive decline and a greater risk of dementia. Follow-up imaging data were available for 408 participants for white matter hyperintensities and 405 participants for fractional anisotropy, allowing researchers to examine how these brain changes progressed over time. The analysis revealed a notable pattern: participants with lower spinal bone density at the beginning of the study tended to experience a faster decline in overall cognitive performance. The researchers also identified changes in specific brain regions that are important for thinking and memory. Lower bone density was associated with greater accumulation of white matter hyperintensities in the corpus callosum, a structure that supports executive function, working memory, and attention. Another connection emerged in the anterior limb of the internal capsule, a brain region involved in executive function. Participants with lower bone density showed a more pronounced decline in fractional anisotropy in this area, suggesting worsening white matter integrity. "This study is the first longitudinal secondary analysis linking baseline vertebral bone mineral density to changes in white matter structure, white matter hyperintensity progression and cognition," Dr. Demehri said. "This comprehensive study using both imaging and clinical assessments sends a clear signal that bone density at baseline is associated with both functional and imaging measures of age-related brain degeneration." Despite the connection between weaker bones and declining brain health, the researchers emphasized that their findings do not establish that osteoporosis causes dementia. Instead, bone deterioration and brain degeneration may be consequences of some of the same biological changes that occur with aging. "This study is not about cause and effect, but rather the observation of a metabolic syndrome that may cause both bone and brain degeneration," Dr. Demehri said. "The co-occurrence observed in the study may reflect shared metabolic drivers of aging, including insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and menopausal change, rather than a direct bone-to-brain effect." These findings raise the possibility that identifying people with reduced bone density could also help recognize those at greater risk of neurological decline. Earlier identification might create opportunities for additional screening and better management of risk factors that affect both skeletal and brain health. One potentially valuable implication of the research is that doctors may be able to obtain useful information about bone density from CT scans that patients have already received for unrelated medical reasons. "Chest CT is done for lung cancer screening, calcium scoring, nodule follow-up, and many other indications," Dr. Momtazmanesh said. "These scans could provide an opportunistic measurement of bone density from the thoracic spine that is associated with a loss of cognitive function." By using AI to analyze existing medical images, researchers may be able to identify patterns of age-related disease that would otherwise go unnoticed. This approach could also help scientists investigate why conditions affecting different parts of the body often develop together. Dr. Demehri concurred: "Diagnostic images contain an immense amount of data that AI can now synthesize at scale across multiple organ systems. This creates a robust, newly feasible opportunity to interconnect co-existing age-related pathologies that have traditionally been studied in isolation and to identify shared biological pathways and potential common causal mechanisms." The study highlights a potentially important connection between bone health and cognitive function, while also demonstrating how AI could make routine medical imaging more informative. Although further research is needed to understand the biological mechanisms involved, the findings suggest that measurements taken from the spine may provide valuable clues about changes occurring in the aging brain. top.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
top.summary: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.
top.text: Researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also prevented severe memory decline in mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Remarkably, the approach relies on mRNA technology similar to that used in COVID-19 vaccines. The discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a new path toward treating conditions that affect the brain. Potential applications extend beyond Alzheimer's disease to other neurodegenerative disorders, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental conditions. "If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely said. The idea behind the research has an unusual origin. The team drew inspiration from Daniel Keyes' science fiction story Flowers for Algernon , which explores the limits of human intelligence through experiments designed to increase intelligence in laboratory mice and people. The treatment works by delivering messenger RNA (mRNA), a type of genetic instruction that tells cells how to produce specific proteins. These instructions are enclosed in tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which protect the mRNA and help it enter cells. Once delivered through the nose, the mRNA instructs cells to manufacture therapeutic proteins capable of reaching the brain. In effect, the nasal tissue becomes a small drug-producing factory, creating substances that can support brain function. "In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime," Professor Neely said. "What's exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic." The study, published in Advanced Science , used mRNA to stimulate production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). This naturally occurring protein helps neurons survive, form connections, and adapt as the brain learns and stores memories. Levels of BDNF tend to decline with aging and are also associated with Alzheimer's disease. The results were striking. Older mice that received the nose drops performed about as well as young mice in standardized tests of working memory, spatial memory, and object recognition. These tests measure abilities such as remembering recently encountered information, navigating surroundings, and recognizing familiar objects. Untreated older animals showed the expected age-related deterioration in cognitive performance. To investigate whether the treatment might also protect against Alzheimer's disease, researchers turned to a widely used laboratory model known as 5XFAD mice. These animals carry genetic mutations that cause them to develop Alzheimer's-like brain changes and memory problems unusually early in life. In this model, signs of Alzheimer's-related brain pathology can typically be detected by two months of age, with measurable cognitive decline appearing around four months. The researchers began administering the BDNF-producing mRNA nose drops when the mice were two months old, around the time the disease-related changes first appeared. Treatment continued twice a week. By four months of age, the treated mice showed no further cognitive decline, unlike the severe deterioration normally seen in this model. The findings suggest that supporting brain cells early in the disease process may help preserve cognitive abilities. One of the most intriguing results was what the treatment did not do. Although memory and learning were protected, the researchers found no reduction in amyloid plaques, the abnormal protein deposits that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. That distinction could be important because many existing Alzheimer's treatments aim to remove amyloid. The new approach instead appears to help neurons remain healthy and functional despite the presence of these deposits. If the same effect can eventually be demonstrated in people, the two treatment strategies might be used together. "Current Alzheimer's treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques," Professor Neely said. "However, just under a third of Alzheimer's patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it's possible to live with Alzheimer's disease pathology." "Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other." Getting medicines into the brain is one of the biggest obstacles in developing treatments for neurological diseases. The blood-brain barrier acts as a protective filter, preventing many potentially harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering delicate brain tissue. Unfortunately, it also blocks numerous drugs that scientists would like to use to treat brain disorders. The nose offers a possible alternative route. Connections between the nasal cavity and the central nervous system may allow certain therapeutic substances to reach the brain without requiring surgery or injections directly into the brain or spinal cord. "This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose," Professor Neely said. The team adapted mRNA technology built on the same clinically validated BioNTech platform used for COVID-19 vaccination. Instead of delivering instructions that prompt an immune response, the modified system provides instructions for producing proteins intended to benefit the brain. First author Dr. Maria Bergamasco, from the University of Sydney's School of Life and Environmental Sciences, explained that the findings illustrate how mRNA technology could be used for purposes far beyond preventing infectious diseases. "The success of mRNA vaccines showed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells," Dr. Bergamasco said. "We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way." The researchers also detected increased neurogenesis, the process through which new neurons are formed, in the hippocampus. This part of the brain plays an essential role in learning and memory and is particularly vulnerable to damage associated with Alzheimer's disease. The increase in new neurons provides another possible explanation for the improvements in cognitive performance. By promoting the health and adaptability of brain cells, BDNF may help maintain the neural networks needed for learning and remembering information. The nose drops also appeared to be well tolerated. Researchers reported no major side effects in the mice during the study, although further testing will be needed to establish long-term safety. Despite the encouraging results, Professor Neely emphasized that the treatment remains experimental. So far, its effectiveness has been demonstrated only in mice, and additional animal safety studies are required before clinical testing can begin. "Before we can trial this therapy in patients, we need to perform a series of safety studies in animals," he said. "It is a very promising pathway, but human noses are different from mouse noses, so we will need to test our drugs in humans before we know whether it will work." top.title: Common sleep and anxiety drugs could be harming aging brains
top.summary: Nearly one in three older adults with dementia or other cognitive disorders takes potentially harmful medications that can worsen brain function and increase the risk of hospitalization and premature death. Despite encouraging progress over the past decade, researchers warn that medication-related harm remains a major and potentially preventable threat to healthy aging.
top.text: Adults age 65 and older who have dementia or other cognitive disorders are particularly vulnerable to the harmful effects of medications used to treat anxiety, sleep disturbances, psychosis, and other conditions affecting the central nervous system. Potential consequences include more emergency room visits, longer and more frequent hospital stays, declining mental health, and an increased risk of premature death. New research from the University at Buffalo (UB) offers some encouraging news, however. Between 2011 and 2022, the proportion of older adults with cognitive disorders taking medications that could impair their cognitive function decreased significantly. After analyzing data from 2,796 older adults with cognitive disorders who lived independently, researchers found that exposure to potentially inappropriate medications fell from 39.3% in 2011 to 29.3% in 2022. "This is a population with some mental issues that relate to the central nervous system. These drugs also act on the central nervous system, so they can be too much for older adults if inappropriately used," says Haowen Hsu, PharmD, a postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Pharmacy Practice at the School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences and first author of the study, published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society . Older adults who have spent years taking benzodiazepines such as Xanax for anxiety or sleep medications such as Ambien may benefit from a medically supervised reduction in dosage or gradual discontinuation. These medications can negatively affect cognitive function, balance, and coordination. "A central word for patients in this age group is 'deprescribing,' which means, for example, removing inappropriate medications and decreasing the frequency or the dosage. In some cases, it means replacing the current medication with a milder alternative," Hsu says. "This is why it's so important for health care providers to work closely with community pharmacists and homecare nurses to optimize medication safety." To identify potentially problematic drugs, the research team consulted the American Geriatrics Society's Beers Criteria, which identifies approximately 100 medications that may pose risks to older adults. The researchers then concentrated specifically on medications that could present additional dangers for people with diagnosed cognitive disorders. Using data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey, the team examined a sample representing approximately 29.7 million older Americans with cognitive disorders over the period from 2011 to 2022. They compared individuals prescribed at least one potentially inappropriate medication with those who had not received any of these drugs. Although the study did not examine what caused the decline in exposure to potentially harmful medications, Hsu points to growing awareness among researchers and clinicians over the past two decades. The gradual but sustained improvement may reflect broader advances in geriatric medicine and efforts to make prescription drug use safer. "We were happy to see the percentages of harm decline over that 11-year period," he says. "However, one-third of our target population is still exposed to these harmful medications, which isn't good." Older adults, even those without cognitive disorders, are particularly susceptible to harmful drug interactions and inappropriate prescriptions. In some cases, these complications can increase the risk of death. These dangers are a central focus of Team Alice, an ongoing interdisciplinary research initiative at the University at Buffalo dedicated to medication safety. Team Alice takes its name from Alice Brennan, who died in 2009 following a prescription for a muscle relaxant identified as potentially inappropriate under the Beers Criteria. The prescribing error went unrecognized within the health care system, and Brennan died following six weeks of preventable complications. Her daughter, Mary Brennan-Taylor, shared her mother's experience with University at Buffalo researchers in the hope of bringing about systemic changes that would spare other patients and families from similar harm. Hsu began the new study shortly after joining the university's pharmacy school and Team Alice, where he works in the UB Patient Safety Learning Laboratory. "This work extends a series of national analyses our group has published on potentially inappropriate medications, quality of life, and health care use in older adults," says David Jacobs, PharmD, PhD, associate professor of pharmacy practice and a principal investigator on Team Alice. "It is especially important as older adults with cognitive disorders are the least able to tolerate medications that worsen memory or thinking, yet nearly one in three are still receiving them. Most of these patients have a regular source of care so these medications can be identified and addressed with their care team." Other contributors to the study included Team Alice's fellow principal investigators Ranjit Singh, MD, associate professor and interim chair of the Department of Family Medicine at UB's Jacobs School of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, and Robert Wahler, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice. Collin Clark, PharmD, clinical associate professor of pharmacy practice, and Steven Feuerstein, an information systems analyst at the Jacobs School, also contributed to the research. The findings underscore the value of thorough medication reviews during routine outpatient appointments. The researchers also suggest incorporating clinical assessment tools such as the Drug Burden Index into acute and outpatient care. Such tools can help health care professionals assess the combined effects of medications that act on the central nervous system and potentially prevent avoidable complications. Further research is needed to establish whether improving medication use can enhance quality of life and reduce hospital admissions and emergency room visits among older adults experiencing cognitive difficulties. The findings arrive at a significant moment in global demographic history. According to a recent report from the U.S. Census Bureau, adults age 65 and older now outnumber children from birth through age 5 worldwide for the first time in human history. However, greater longevity does not necessarily translate into more years of good health. The same report indicates that nearly 75% of adults age 65 and older have at least two chronic health conditions. Managing multiple illnesses often requires taking more medications, some of which may have detrimental effects on the aging body and brain. "This is an issue that has been building for decades, but the growth of the older adult population has arrived sooner than we expected," Hsu says. "This means that health care professionals need to pay closer attention than ever to medication safety, especially for older adults experiencing cognitive decline or other complex health concerns." top.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
top.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.
top.text: A small fossil discovered in Scotland and regarded for nearly three decades as one of the earliest known reptiles has turned out to be a very different kind of prehistoric animal. New research published in Nature is challenging its long-established place in evolutionary history. The study was led by scientists at the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working in collaboration with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility. The 345-million-year-old fossil, discovered in 1984, belongs to a species called Westlothiana lizziae . Nicknamed "Lizzie" because of its resemblance to a lizard, the specimen consists of a nearly complete skeleton preserved in two crushed slabs of rock. Early descriptions relied largely on anatomical features visible at the surface, including four limbs with fingers and toes that appeared to have claw-like tips. These characteristics distinguished Westlothiana from many other animals living at the time, whose limbs more closely resembled fins. Although the fossil's distorted condition made its anatomy difficult to interpret, researchers widely regarded it as the earliest known amniote adapted to life on land. Amniotes are a major group of vertebrates that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals. Following its scientific description in 1990, Westlothiana became an important reference point for researchers investigating when and how these animals first evolved. "Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades," said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum's Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. "But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected." Using powerful X-ray imaging technology at the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, the scientists peered beneath the surface of the rock and reconstructed previously inaccessible parts of the animal's anatomy. What they discovered was strikingly different from the anatomy expected in an early reptile. Lizzie possessed a primitive skull, internal gills containing bone, and a mouth resembling that of a fish, complete with thousands of tiny teeth. Together, these features rule out its previously proposed position within the evolutionary lineage leading to reptiles. Instead of living primarily on land, Westlothiana appears to have been an aquatic or amphibious animal. "The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought," said Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford. The discovery also changes how scientists understand the origins of several anatomical features traditionally associated with vertebrates adapted to terrestrial environments. Researchers now believe that characteristics such as claws and the arrangement of five digits on each hand and foot, a pattern familiar in reptiles and mammals, had already emerged in earlier animals that were still closely associated with water. These creatures belonged to the evolutionary lineage leading to tetrapods, the broader group of four-limbed vertebrates that encompasses both amphibians and amniotes. "This is a big surprise," said study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum's Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. "It shows that, although we think of amphibians as being more 'primitive' than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles." The findings could also have important implications for the interpretation of prehistoric fossil tracks. Recently discovered trackways have been used as evidence that amniotes first appeared during the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago. These ancient impressions record the movements of a four-limbed animal with apparently clawed digits. However, if distant relatives of tetrapods such as Westlothiana also possessed claws, such footprints are no longer sufficient on their own to identify the animals that left them as amniotes. Some trackways previously attributed to early amniotes may instead have been left by more ancient, amphibious creatures belonging to the evolutionary lineage of tetrapods. "The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water," Jenkins said. Additional contributors to the study include Jason Head from the University of Cambridge, Vincent Fernandez from the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility, Lucy Roberts from the Natural History Museum, London, and Timothy Smithson from the University Museum of Zoology Cambridge.
