top.title: An unexpected link: More coarse particles in indoor air, lower odds of Kawasaki disease
top.summary: Kawasaki disease (KD) is an acute inflammatory condition that primarily affects children under 5. It causes inflammation of blood vessels throughout the body and can lead to serious complications, particularly affecting the coronary arteries that supply blood to the heart. Although Kawasaki disease is a major cause of acquired heart disease in children, its exact cause remains unclear. Genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures are thought to contribute to its development, but the underlying mechanisms are not fully understood.

top.title: Frontal brain regions reveal an unexpected eye for detail outside the visual cortex
top.summary: The first time Bilal Haider saw the recordings, he thought something had gone wrong. Haider has spent his career studying vision, trying to understand how the brain transforms light hitting the retina into the rich visual world we experience: a face, a tree, an object moving across a room.

top.title: Trial finds no benefit from prehospital antibiotics for sepsis
top.summary: For patients with suspected sepsis, early antibiotic treatment is considered critical for reducing mortality. But a new study has found that earlier treatment with antibiotics in an ambulance did not reduce mortality compared with standard sepsis care in the emergency department (ED), researchers reported in JAMA.

top.title: No, eating celery won't make you lose weight. How we fell for the myth of negative calories
top.summary: Back in my early days as a dietitian, I used to hear about the miracle properties of celery.

top.title: Existing drug helps mice clear blood through meningeal lymphatic system after stroke
top.summary: A drug already used to improve blood circulation and prevent certain types of stroke could have an unexpected new role in promoting recovery after bleeding in the brain. In a study published in Stroke, a team led by researchers at National Taiwan University found that cilostazol helped mice recover from intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) by boosting the brain's natural drainage system.

top.title: When's a new organ not really new? Two anatomists explain
top.summary: People have been dissecting the human body for more than 2,500 years. In recent times, we've been over every nanometer with high-resolution medical imaging. So you'd think we know all there is to know about human anatomy. Surely, there are no new organs left to discover.

top.title: The child development 'sweet spot' that affects adult taste preference
top.summary: A baby's transition from breast milk or formula to a range of solid foods is the likely "sweet spot" for introducing nutritional variety that influences lifelong taste preferences by rewiring circuits in the brain, new research in mice suggests.

top.title: Adolescent and teen depression linked to heavier substance use
top.summary: Adolescents and teenagers who drink more alcohol or use multiple forms of marijuana are much more likely to experience major depression. In addition, girls, older teens and multiracial teens are more likely to experience major depression, regardless of drug or alcohol use.

top.title: Resistance training could help boost brain health and confidence in older adults
top.summary: Think about the last time you stood up from a chair or lifted a heavy shopping bag from the floor. These movements might feel automatic, but they take a surprising amount of coordination between your brain and your muscles.

top.title: New liver model for studying alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency
top.summary: AATD is a rare genetic metabolic disorder that affects the liver and lungs. A mutation causes liver cells (hepatocytes) to form misfolded alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT). This misfolding results in reduced secretion of AAT into the blood plasma. AAT plays an important role in controlling inflammatory processes in the body by mitigating excessive reactions that lead to tissue damage.

top.title: A protein in the brain's immune cells may accelerate damage in Alzheimer's disease
top.summary: Researchers at Lund University in Sweden have identified a key role for the protein galectin-3 in Alzheimer's disease. The study shows that galectin-3 not only influences how the brain's immune cells, known as microglia, react to the disease's characteristic amyloid plaques but also shapes the plaques themselves—and may contribute to the nerve damage that develops around them.

top.title: Despite soaring demand for GLP-1s, many eligible patients are unable to access these drugs for weight loss
top.summary: In just a few short years, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists have surged in popularity across the United States, transforming from specialized treatments for type 2 diabetes into revolutionary therapeutics for weight management, cardiovascular health and other emerging uses. But not all populations are benefiting from this expansion. As GLP-1 use has increased, disparities in access to these drugs have widened significantly, according to a new study led by researchers at Boston University School of Public Health (BUSPH).

top.title: Some people claim to speak many languages. But what does it really mean to be a polyglot?
top.summary: Roughly half of the world's population speaks more than one language. But speaking two or three languages is very different from claiming proficiency in five, 10 or more.

top.title: A fungus that can survive in Chernobyl could help create materials that trap and break down nerve agents and pesticides
top.summary: Deep inside the Chernobyl exclusion zone, where radiation levels have remained unsafe for people for the past 40 years, black molds climb the walls of the damaged former nuclear plant in Ukraine. They're entirely undeterred by the radiation—in fact, some fungi even grow toward it.

top.title: California raised minimum wages for fast‑food workers—here's how it played out 2 years later
top.summary: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers' purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.

top.title: Self-assembling nanocarriers show promise for delivering CRISPR to tumors and slowing growth
top.summary: A self-assembling supramolecular nanocarrier protects Cas9 RNPs from degradation, enhances systemic delivery and preferential tumor accumulation, and enables pH-responsive intracellular release. top.title: Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials
top.summary: The mpox curve has started to rise again, with cases concentrated in Rio and São Paulo. There is no available treatment for this virus strain, which is different from the one in the 2022 outbreak.
top.text: The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox , an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026. Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness. The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17 , which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year. The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23 , compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022. The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak. In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb. In response, the Ministry of Health purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease and instructed states and municipalities to administer it intradermally – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold. The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just failed two clinical trials . Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024. Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs. At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, 43 of the 62 samples identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb. Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases. Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first cases with evidence of community transmission – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026. The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care. In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV. During the 2022 outbreak, the antiviral drug tecovirimat was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U.S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been eradicated from the planet since 1980 . But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people. An April 2025 trial compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant. In February 2026, a second trial settled the question regarding clade II . The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox. Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients. The only vaccine for mpox is MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos , a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, observational studies conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes. Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two , compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses . In the U.S., a cohort of at-risk transgender men and women estimated 89% protection with the full vaccination series and 70% with a single dose. In another study in Germany, the effectiveness of a single dose was 58% overall, but only 35% among people living with HIV – a relevant finding for Brazil, given that nearly half of Brazilian cases occur in patients with HIV. This study also found that in those who have already been exposed, the vaccine reduces the risk of becoming ill by about 20% and appears to lessen the severity of the illness even when it does not prevent infection. There are two weaknesses in these studies. The first concerns the duration of protection: Antibody levels drop sharply between six and 12 months after the second dose, although the cellular response persists. It is not yet known which of these indicators is a better predictor of protection. The second is that there is no data on clinical efficacy against clade Ib, though there are laboratory studies. A British group showed in April 2026 that serum from 25 vaccinated healthcare workers neutralizes clade Ib , but at levels consistently lower than those observed against clade IIb. Cross-protection is likely, based on animal models challenged with clade I. The extent of this protection in humans, however, is unknown. The intradermal injection method, now recommended by Brazil’s Ministry of Health, was adopted in the United States and Europe in 2022 – this method allows the use of one-fifth of the dose – and produced an immune response comparable to that of the subcutaneous method. The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025.
In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17 , which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year.
The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23 , compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022.
The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.

Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024.

Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.
Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026.

top.title: Ancient Cahokia transformed amid droughts and flooding—climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
top.summary: More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.

top.title: Artificial photosynthesis uses waste CO₂ to grow protein-rich edible fungus in seven days
top.summary: While many people think first of meat when they think about dietary protein, most protein ultimately depends on plants, since livestock feed on grass, hay and other plants. Meeting the demand for protein is taxing on the environment, requiring massive amounts of land and water while creating greenhouse gas emissions. And that demand is expected to require nearly 50% more agricultural production by 2050 than in 2012, according to the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization.

top.title: Certain fungi turn specialized plant cells into water-carrying cells using one protein
top.summary: Can a pathogen that causes damage to a plant also make that plant more resilient to drought? An international research team led by the University of Göttingen has investigated this apparent paradox. The researchers discovered how certain fungi promote the formation of new water-conducting cells in plants. At the same time, infected plants showed increased tolerance to drought stress. The results were published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe.

top.title: The dark matter puzzle deepens: Nearby galaxies challenge cosmic simulations
top.summary: Galaxies appear to hold a surprise beneath their visible stars: Their inner regions contain less dark matter than some of our most advanced simulations predict. Dark matter is invisible, but its gravitational pull helps govern the motions of stars and gas. By measuring these movements, astronomers can reconstruct where this unseen matter lies and test the computer simulations used to understand the universe. A study of 136 nearby galaxies, involving the Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC), reveals a discrepancy that becomes more extensive in more massive systems, offering fresh clues about how galaxies form and evolve.

top.title: 3D modeling questions Viking 'fast fashion'
top.summary: High-resolution 3D modeling of Viking brooches and the molds used to make them identifies surprisingly few matches between them, indicating the brooches were not mass-produced, as previously thought, but instead made by individual, creative artisans.

top.title: Climate communication that resonates must be based on empathy
top.summary: Climate change is a global reality, but people often encounter it through different local realities. For some, it enters everyday life through social media feeds, news reports, scientific findings and public discussion. For others, it is through water scarcity, food insecurity, floods, heat waves, wildfires or the loss of a home or a loved one.

top.title: Putting Google's AI hurricane model to the test
top.summary: A week before Hurricane Melissa slammed into Jamaica last fall, the forecast models couldn't agree on where it was headed or how strong it would get. One got it right—an AI model from Google DeepMind, which called both the storm's path and its Category 5 strength.

top.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
top.summary: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America. Each person completed a standard loneliness questionnaire, then chose between ordinary products and versions that cost 15% to 20% more but carried an ethical or environmental label. Items included toothpaste, chocolate bars, jackets and backpacks.

top.title: Whether it’s ‘Sister’ or your own sister, the burden that caring for aging parents puts on women is no joke
top.summary: About 1 in 4 US adults are family caregivers.
top.text: “Sister,” the “Saturday Night Live” sketch about daughters who take care of their aging parents, hit home for a lot of people . The make-believe ad features several men who say they love their father but don’t want to interrupt their own lives to help him or deal with his chronic health conditions. So they’ve turned to a handy service, which costs nothing, by texting “Dad fell” to their sister. “Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow not yours,” a man in a doctor-evoking white coat explains. I winced as I watched the sketch because my own sister, Carol, provided full-time, unpaid care for our mother for more than a decade. In 2018, when I wrote about the daunting economics of caregiving for older adults for The Conversation, I led with Carol’s story. One reason “Sister,” which stars Jane Wickline as an exhausted caregiver and John Mulaney as her smug brother, packed such a big punch is that more of us find ourselves in her shoes. My sister was one of 43.5 million Americans providing care to a loved one at the time. That number has since risen to 63 million – about 1 in 4 adults. The care family members provide today, as it was in 2018, is mostly unpaid. And it’s labor that isn’t counted when the government estimates the scale of economic activity. That doesn’t mean it’s not valuable work – estimates put its value at about US$1 trillion . Family caregivers make it possible for many older people to remain in their homes. That, in turn, can make an aging person happier and reduces the costs of their stays in hospitals and nursing homes. But their freedom to age in place comes at a price. Caregiving is tough work, and numerous studies over the years have found that caregivers suffer more physical and emotional stress than other people. That’s why at the end of the “Sister” ad, the announcer speaks in the rapid-fire speedtalking normally reserved for a drug’s unpleasant side effects as he cautions: “Sister may break down without warning.” Caregiving may save money that might otherwise be spent on home health aides or assisted living fees, both of which are beyond the means of many families. The average cost of in-home care is $35 per hour , totaling over $25,000 a month for 24/7 care. Compare that to a median annual household income of $87,460 . But it is costly for the caregivers to do this unpaid work for their parents or other loved ones. Over 90% of caregivers must cut their work hours ), which typically reduces their wages, employer-provided retirement benefits and Social Security benefits. Some of them, like “Sister” in the sketch – and my own sister – end up quitting their paid jobs to do this unpaid one. AARP estimates that family caregivers who were born between 1981 and 1985 and are in the paid workforce will lose on average $120,500 in income over their lifetimes because of their time devoted to caregiving. Caregivers also incur over $7,000 annually on average in out-of-pocket expenses for home modifications and other caregiving necessities. Sociologists have found that men with a sister do less parental caregiving than men without a sister. They have also found that women with a brother do more caregiving than women without a brother. This extra caregiving burden women face is sometimes called the “ daughterhood penalty ,” or tax. Social psychologists Toni Schmader and Katharina Block explain the various ways children are taught that caring is a feminine trait and being uncaring is masculine, although there’s no obvious gender differences in caregiving ability. Economists’ explanations of gender differences in employment and earnings initially focused on differences in education and experience. Now, economists like me also recognize the role that social norms play in determining who works in certain jobs and how much they’re paid, including who in the family will take care of aging relatives. But there is some good news – if not for “Sister,” then for some other sisters out there: growing evidence that the gender gap in caregiving is narrowing. Female caregivers who belong to the baby boom generation – people born 1944-1964 – spent three times more time doing household chores than their male counterparts, according to a study published in 2024. This gender difference was much smaller among caregivers who were millennials – people born 1980-1985, mostly because women in that generation spent less time doing household chores.

top.title: How to protect your retirement savings if the AI boom fizzles
top.summary: Many savers don’t know how much of their 401(k) funds are weighted toward Big Tech companies.
top.text: After stock markets, including the tech-heavy NASDAQ, got pummeled on Nov. 20, 2026, many Americans are asking themselves whether the huge bet on artificial intelligence is heading south. While markets rebounded the following Monday, this question still has profound implications for retirement savings, given how much these investment accounts are tied to stocks . Before Monday’s surge, the NASDAQ had plunged about 18% since early October and had lost more than US$4 trillion since Nov. 16. The broad-based S&P 500 also took a beating and had shed all its gains for the year. As a finance professor and certified financial planner, I can’t tell you whether the bubble has truly burst for good. But I can explain how the default model that most 401(k) plans use works, where it protects you, and what you might consider changing. Whether AI stocks recover or not, the steps that protect a retirement account are the same: Know what you own, keep the mix of assets in balance, and hold enough in savings and low-risk funds to cover the years when you’ll need it. Most 401(k) savers hold a target-date fund , which is named for the year of your “target” retirement and is often chosen as a default option by the employer. To understand how the current stock market volatility affects retirement savings, it’s important to first explain how these funds work. About 55% of U.S. families have a defined contribution retirement account, such as a 401(k) or an individual retirement account. And inside a 401(k), the investing is increasingly done for you. Six in 10 plans administered by the fund giant Vanguard signed workers up automatically in 2025 when they started a new job. And when those plans set a default investment, 98% of savers choose a target-date fund . About 60% of the nearly 5 million savers in those plans held a single target-date fund and nothing else. Taken together, target-date funds now hold $4.8 trillion . Inside each target-date fund is a list of index funds, which are named so because they track a particular market index. Vanguard’s series, the largest, is built mainly from four indices : U.S. stocks, international stocks, U.S. bonds and international bonds. The mix changes the older the saver gets, gradually moving away from high-return, high-risk stocks to safer, lower-yielding bonds. For example, Vanguard’s 2055 fund was just over 91% stocks at the end of September 2026, reflecting the relative youth of those holding it. That share drops to 16% for savers invested in the 2027 fund , who expect to retire imminently. That autopilot model is now being tested, starting with Nvidia. In the span of a week, Nvidia went from riding the AI boom to getting mired in crisis. On Nov. 5, after the U.S. midterm elections raised the prospect of new curbs on AI and data centers , Nvidia shares fell more than 9%, while the broad-based S&P 500 index lost 4.4% . Then, on Nov. 12, Nvidia announced that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned . By the end of that week, Nvidia had lost more than $1 trillion in market value within a month. That slide may now be reversed. Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Nov. 23, causing its share price to soar. More broadly, it’s too early to say whether the AI bubble is over. Some analysts argue that it’s just losing some air rather than bursting. But amid the turmoil in tech stocks, savers may wonder whether a retirement plan on autopilot should adjust to this fresh volatility. Target-date funds are marketed as broadly diversified, often holding thousands of stocks, and financial advisers repeated that point after Huang’s exit. But those stocks aren’t held in equal amounts. Index funds weight companies by market value. So as the value of AI-linked companies soared, their share has grown in the funds most 401(k) savers hold . And that gets to the question of whether there’s a tech bubble riding on overvalued AI companies. By the end of 2025, the 10 largest companies made up nearly 41% of the S&P 500 , according to RBC Wealth Management. Yet those 10, almost all of which are in tech and AI, were expected to produce only about 32% of the index’s 2025 earnings. In other words, investors are paying a premium for these shares because they’re expecting great profits later. Bad news can shrink that premium quickly. Savers should also know that a target-date fund dilutes the concentration of AI stocks, but it doesn’t remove them. At the end of September, the 10 largest companies made up 36% of Vanguard’s total U.S. stock fund , with Nvidia at 7%. A 2055 fund keeps about 55% of its money there. So roughly 20 cents of every dollar was riding on 10 companies, and about 4 cents on Nvidia. That means even a small drop in these stocks can have a big impact on your fund, depending on its asset mix. And while diversification hedges against one company’s turmoil, it’s less helpful if there’s a broad repricing of tech stocks. Even in Vanguard’s international fund, the four largest holdings are all tied to chipmaking, led by Taiwan Semiconductor, which makes Nvidia’s chips. Furthermore, diversification doesn’t mean guaranteed protection all the time. In 2008, during the global financial crisis, funds built for people retiring in 2010 lost nearly 24% on average . In principle, savers don’t need to do anything as long as they choose to stay on autopilot until retirement. Fund managers buy and sell assets to stick to the target mix – a practice known as rebalancing. But rebalancing resets only the broad categories rather than trimming one particular company for growing too large. As Nvidia’s share of the market rose, so did its share of the fund. For people who hold just one target-date fund, I believe the right response to this month’s news is to leave their 401(k) account alone . The fund has been rebalancing all along, and your stake in any one company is modest. First, consider the year you expect to retire. If you want to move it earlier or later, or want more or less risk, you should choose a fund with a different year. Second, look at what the fund’s share of stocks is today, which is on the fund’s fact sheet. If you’re 60 and your fund is 60% stocks, a 30% fall in stocks would cut your balance by roughly 18%. If that would derail your retirement plans, you can switch to an earlier-dated fund that holds less in stocks and brings less risk. Third, if you have other funds, you should review them. About 1 in 4 target-date investors in Vanguard plans hold other funds. If you add a tech fund or an S&P 500 fund, your account is riskier and more concentrated than the label suggests. About 31% of savers in Vanguard plans opt out of target-date funds and choose their own investments, perhaps because they find target-date funds too conservative or their fees too costly . For these investors, and for anyone with old 401(k)s and IRAs, there is more to do. Start by looking at the fact sheet for each fund, like this one for Vanguard’s S&P 500 index fund , and compare the top holdings. An S&P 500 index fund, a large-cap growth fund and a technology or Nasdaq-tracking fund look like three investments. But in fact you may own the same handful of companies three times. Next, you should rebalance your holdings according to your plan, not to a prediction. That means returning to the mix of stocks and bonds that you chose in the first place. Trades inside a 401(k) don’t trigger taxes, and many plans offer automatic rebalancing. If yours doesn’t, a simple rule backed by Vanguard research works: review once or twice a year, and rebalance whenever any part of your mix drifts more than about 5 percentage points from your target. Finally, consider broadening the stocks you own. Morningstar Indexes strategist Dan Lefkovitz has pointed to U.S. value stocks, smaller companies and international stocks as areas with less AI exposure. Your plan may offer funds for each. None of these makes you immune to losses, and diversifying can mean trailing the hottest part of the market for years. Bu

top.title: A doctor’s guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP-1 medication
top.summary: By minding your body’s fullness cues you can indulge in your favorite holiday foods and traditions while maintaining your progress with these drugs.
top.text: Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends. But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts. For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different. As a physician specializing in obesity medicine , I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage. However, these medications don’t eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love. Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes , obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb. GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients feel full sooner and stay full longer . Many patients also report fewer cravings for high-calorie foods and even a reduced desire to drink alcohol . In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they’re satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging. One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body’s changing fullness signals . Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate. These symptoms can serve as reminders that you’ve reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving. GLP-1 medications don’t make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors. Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and celebrations often revolve around drinking . Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience. Some patients report that GLP-1 medications reduce their desire for alcohol altogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment. Alcohol can worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications. If you choose to drink, consider these precautions: Limit your intake. Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication. Avoid drinking on an empty stomach. Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal. Pay attention to how you feel. Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms. The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms. Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment. Plan ahead for medication storage. Some injectable GLP-1 medications require refrigeration before use, while others allow room-temperature storage for a specified period after dispensing or first use. Storage requirements vary considerably by product. Check the prescribing information for your specific medication or ask your pharmacist before traveling. Don’t assume that all injectable medications can remain unrefrigerated for the same length of time. If you’re flying, keep your medication and supplies in your carry-on luggage. This helps protect them from extreme temperatures and prevents problems if your checked luggage gets delayed or lost. Keep in mind that you might also need to have a note from your prescribing provider to carry them on. Arrange prescription refills in advance. If you anticipate needing a refill while traveling, contact your pharmacy and prescribing clinician ahead of time. Prescribing and dispensing regulations can complicate obtaining medications in another state, so don’t wait until you run out. Stick to your regular dosing schedule. Don’t take an extra dose or double up on medication to accommodate a holiday meal or try to suppress your appetite further. Taking more medication than prescribed can increase the risk of significant side effects and potentially cause an overdose . If travel disrupts your dosing schedule or you miss a dose, follow the instructions for your specific medication, or contact your prescribing clinician or pharmacist. When in doubt, plan ahead and ask for guidance rather than making medication adjustments on your own. Perhaps the most important advice I give my patients is this: The holidays are not everyday life, and one large meal or dessert will not erase the progress you’ve made. You don’t need to skip Thanksgiving dinner, avoid your favorite dessert or feel guilty about enjoying a special meal. Maintaining a healthy relationship with food means allowing yourself flexibility while keeping your long-term goals in perspective. At the same time, don’t let one celebratory meal turn into several weeks of abandoning the habits that have helped you succeed. Enjoy the occasion, recognize when you’ve had enough, and return to your usual routine afterward.
